overview: This 236-page file traces Japanese military movements in China and Northeast Asia from the Manchurian Incident of 1931 through the expanding Sino-Japanese War in 1938. State Department telegrams, consular despatches, military intelligence reports, memoranda, and filing sheets document railway-borne advances and occupations in Manchuria; reinforcements, combat deployments, and the negotiated withdrawal from Shanghai in 1932; subsequent concentrations near Harbin, Jehol, the Soviet frontier, and Outer Mongolia; and large troop embarkations from Japan in 1938. Collectively, the documents show how American diplomats and military observers monitored Japanese force strength, transport networks, command arrangements, operational intentions, and the restoration—or continued denial—of Chinese authority.
interest: The file is especially useful for reconstructing the logistics and tempo of Japanese expansion: individual trains, river steamers, troop landings, divisional transfers, and local garrisons appear alongside broader estimates of strategy and force strength. Its unusually detailed coverage of the 1932 Shanghai evacuation records the town-by-town handover to Chinese police and civil authorities, revealing how an armistice worked on the ground. Reports from diplomats, attachés, eyewitness observers, and the press also permit historians to compare verified movements with rumors, propaganda, and official explanations, while the later documents connect the crises of 1931–1933 to Japan’s wider military mobilization by 1938.
